Al-Shahrastānī himself also emphasizes the same interpenetration when he compares the relation to water in a rose, oil in sesame, and butterfat in milk.
But if spirit and body interpenetrate one another in this way, the idea that the body is merely an instrument or mold becomes difficult to maintain. The two ideas almost contradict each other.

We can therefore say that al-Shahrastānī introduces a tension into his own account by first speaking of the body as an instrument and mold and then describing spirit and body as interpenetrating one another like water in a rose, oil in sesame, or butterfat in milk.
Apart from this, al-Ashʿarī and al-Shahrastānī agree that al-Naẓẓām treated the spirit as a body.
Al-Ashʿarī alone, however, records several other important details about al-Naẓẓām’s doctrine.
Because al-Ashʿarī lived earlier than al-Shahrastānī and was much closer in time to al-Naẓẓām himself, we will rely mainly on his account when trying to reconstruct al-Naẓẓām’s position.
What can we draw from the two passages preserved by al-Ashʿarī?
First, al-Naẓẓām treats the spirit or soul as material. Both al-Ashʿarī and al-Shahrastānī agree that he called the spirit a body.

Second, he presents the relation between body and spirit as one of interpenetration and interweaving, to the point that “all of this is in all of that,” as al-Ashʿarī puts it, or that the spirit is in the body “as water is in a rose,” as al-Shahrastānī says.
The two images express essentially the same idea.
But how should we understand this relationship between spirit and body?
Is it a relationship between two separate things, so that al-Naẓẓām is ultimately defending a dualism of spirit and body—a position whose basic character belongs to idealist thought?
Or is it a single unified relationship that rules out dualism altogether?
The explanatory images used by both historians point more strongly toward a unified whole than toward a strict dualism.

Unfortunately, we have no surviving text by al-Naẓẓām himself that would allow us to settle the matter directly. Nothing from his theories has reached us except through historians of Arab philosophy and historians of Islamic sects.

Whatever al-Naẓẓām’s exact understanding of the relationship between spirit and body may have been, his statement that the spirit is a body still points toward philosophical starting points marked by a materialist tendency.
That tendency takes forms particular to his own historical setting, a setting still deeply shaped by metaphysical and idealist ideas.
Third, al-Ashʿarī tells us that al-Naẓẓām denied that “life and power are meanings separate from the living and powerful being.”

This confirms the same Aristotelian idea we saw in his statement that “length is the long thing and width is the wide thing”: essence does not exist independently in its own right. What actually exists are the concrete things in which that essence appears.
Fourth, we come to al-Naẓẓām’s statement that:

The spirit exists in the body in such a way that the body is an affliction upon it and a cause that leads it to choose. If the spirit were freed from the body, its actions would take place by generation and necessity.
According to al-Ashʿarī’s account, this means that the spirit’s presence in the body creates a kind of interpenetration between opposites—the body being an “affliction” upon the spirit.
The presence of the spirit in the body is what makes bodily actions voluntary. In other words, it gives rise to the consciousness through which a human being can choose.

If the spirit were to leave the body, the actions produced by the body would instead become necessary. They would arise naturally, mechanically, and automatically, like the actions of non-human or non-living things.
A stone, for example, produces a sound when it falls or strikes another hard object.
What do we find in this view?
In reality, idealist and materialist tendencies are mixed together here so closely that it becomes difficult to separate one from the other.
The idea that the body is an affliction upon the spirit has a familiar mystical tone. To some extent, it recalls the Neoplatonic idea of an upward and downward pull between body and spirit.
From this side, the view belongs quite clearly to idealist thought.
But from another side, the same statement contains an idea of the unity of opposites in the joining of the spirit with what is described as its affliction, the body.

From a third side, al-Naẓẓām gives consciousness a central role in distinguishing human beings from other forms of existence. He gives the spirit the character of consciousness, and through that consciousness the human being possesses will and choice.
Yet from a fourth side, the same view still suggests a dualism between spirit and body, and as we have said, dualism is fundamentally an idealist idea.
But this brings us back to the point we made earlier.

Among thinkers and philosophers who lived in an age such as al-Naẓẓām’s and developed their ideas within a religious framework, it is extremely difficult to find a materialist tendency completely free of idealist elements.
E — Al-Jāḥiẓ reports that al-Naẓẓām said:

The soul perceives sensible things through these openings: the ear, the mouth, the nose, and the eye. It is not that the human being possesses a hearing faculty separate from himself or a sight faculty separate from himself. The human being hears by himself, though he may become deaf because of some injury that affects him. In the same way, he sees by himself, though he may become blind because of an injury.
To us today, this statement may seem almost too obvious to be worth making.
But al-Naẓẓām was not simply stating something everyone in his time already accepted. We cannot take the statement out of its historical setting.
In his age, different schools, sects, and thinkers disagreed sharply over the nature of the senses. Many even denied the senses in one form or another.
Al-Ashʿarī says that among these were thinkers who denied the existence of accidents.
He also reports that the Marcionites held that the body contains a spirit and five senses, with the spirit being something different from both the senses and the body.

The Manichaeans, he says, held that the human being is the five senses, that these senses are bodies, and that nothing exists beyond them. For them, reality consisted of two things: light and darkness.
Light had five senses, and darkness had five senses: hearing, sight, taste, smell, and touch.
The Dayṣānites, by contrast, said that darkness is dead and ignorant and has no sensation, while light is alive in itself and capable of sensation.

They held that light’s hearing is the same thing as its sight, taste, and smell. Only the direction of perception differs, so that it perceives through one direction what it does not perceive through another.
And there were many other strange views of the same kind.

Once we picture this mixture of doctrines about the senses, their perceptions, their relationship to spirit and body, and their connection with theories of knowledge, we can better understand the progressive significance of al-Naẓẓām’s position.
Within this confused field of competing views, he returned the senses to their organic basis in the human being and recognized both their bodily function and their role in knowledge.
Seen in this historical setting, the question was not nearly as obvious as it seems to us today.
But we still need to look carefully at al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “the soul perceives sensible things through these openings.”
Does this mean that he denies the senses any role in knowledge because he assigns sensory perception to the soul, acting through the “openings” of the ear, mouth, nose, and eye?
The issue seems largely one of wording.
As we saw earlier, for al-Naẓẓām the soul or spirit is the human being.
So it is the human being who perceives sensible things through these five senses.
And that is indeed the case.
Even if al-Naẓẓām believed that the senses had no existence independent of the human being, would that mean that he denied their role in knowledge?
Or could they still remain the means through which sensory knowledge is acquired, whether or not they exist independently?
F — In the debates over accidents, al-Naẓẓām also disagreed with his teacher Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.
Al-ʿAllāf held that an accident could exist without being in a body and that an event could occur without being in a place.
Al-Naẓẓām denied both possibilities. He rejected the idea that an accident could exist outside a place or come into being outside a body.
Al-Ashʿarī tells us that many speculative thinkers agreed with him.
It should be clear that here too al-Naẓẓām remains consistent with the materialist tendency we have tried to draw out from his different views.
This position follows naturally from his theory of motion.
For al-Naẓẓām, motion is the only real accident belonging to bodies, and all other accidents arise from it.
He also holds that something moving cannot move “in nothing” or “toward nothing”—in other words, that it cannot move outside space and time.
Given these premises, he is entirely consistent when he rejects the possibility that an accident could exist without a place or occur without a body.
At the end of this examination of al-Naẓẓām, and after trying to identify the intellectual basis from which his various positions develop, we can now draw a more general conclusion about him.

His thinking shows enough consistency for us to say that the materialist tendency visible across his philosophical views was not merely an isolated tendency that appeared in one question and disappeared in another.

When we follow his ideas from one subject to the next, he seems to have built a reasonably coherent system of ideas, positions, and concepts around several of the major questions debated and investigated in his time.
But we are certainly not claiming that al-Naẓẓām consciously understood this tendency as leading him toward a definite position in the continuing objective conflict between materialism and idealism.
Finally, we should explain why we have spent so much time on al-Naẓẓām.

To study him at length is really to study an entire philosophical current within Muʿtazilite thought, a current associated with his name and one that had a deep influence during the third and fourth centuries of the Islamic calendar.
The Social Basis of the Muʿtazilite Idea of Divine Unity
Up to this point, in our discussion of the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity, we have examined the main areas of Muʿtazilite thought connected with that principle, whether directly or indirectly.
What was the relationship between this intellectual doctrine of divine unity, in all its different theoretical forms, and its social basis?
In other words, what was its relationship to the ideological side of Islam?
After traveling through such a wide area of Muʿtazilite thought in this chapter, it may seem that we have moved very far away from that social and ideological foundation.

That impression may become even stronger because our discussion has taken us deep into questions that can look like purely metaphysical mazes, almost completely cut off from the world of human social activity.

When Muʿtazilite thinkers debated the divine “attributes” and all the purely metaphysical problems surrounding them, were they thinking about these questions in complete isolation from the social world in which they lived?
At the beginning of the next chapter, which we will turn to shortly, we will answer this question.
The answer will show that these thinkers never truly left their human and social world behind.
Their engagement with metaphysical questions was not a withdrawal of thought from that world.
On the contrary, it was one particular way of taking part in it.
Their engagement was an intellectual struggle to develop a rational form for the basic principles on which the ideology of Islam rested.
If we look closely at the direction taken by Muʿtazilite discussions of the divine “attributes”—the group of questions centered on the principle of divine unity—the picture becomes clearer.

All this intense intellectual effort was directed toward establishing divine unity on an extremely firm foundation: the absolute transcendence of God, placing the divine being completely beyond comparison with the created world and completely above it.
This absolute transcendence stood at the center of the ideology of Islam—that is, of the social and political order of the Islamic state.

The social, or more precisely social-political, meaning of this transcendent concept of divine unity, as the Muʿtazilites developed it, pointed toward an image of an enormous distance between the person at the head of the Islamic state—the caliph—and the institutions of the state on one side, and the human members of Arab-Islamic society on the other.
That distance mirrored the vast separation between the transcendent and unique divine being and our material world.
This was the basic foundation of the ideological structure of the caliphal state.

Does this mean, then, that when the Muʿtazilites struggled intellectually to establish divine unity on the basis of absolute transcendence, they were also helping to create an ideology of absolute separation between the head of the caliphal system and the society ruled by that system—between an absolute ruler and those he ruled?
Broadly speaking, there is no doubt that they moved within the limits of this ideology, whether they intended to or not, and whether they were conscious of it or not.

The social and intellectual conditions of their time, and the objective historical relationships within those conditions, placed them in a position to produce the ideology of the caliphal system in a rational form.

But because thought has its own internal movement and a degree of relative independence, producing the ideology of the system in this rational form also meant producing contradictions within that ideology at the same time.
We have already seen several examples of this contradiction in the present chapter on divine unity.
The most important was the breakthrough made in what we might call the Islamic theory of knowledge.
